46202: Biblical Hermeneutics: How to Read the Bible Well
46203: A plain-language deep study of interpretation: methods, history, genres, context, the Jewish covenant lens, Christ, the Spirit and the community
46204: Hermeneutics is the study of how we understand and apply a text. Everyone who reads the Bible interprets it, so the real question is whether we do it carefully or carelessly. Reading well means listening first to what a passage meant to its first hearers: its kind of writing (genre), the words around it, and its Jewish and ancient setting. Then we place it inside the Bible's one big covenant story, see how it points to or is fulfilled in Jesus, and ask what it calls us to do today, together with other believers. Christians have read Scripture in different ways across history, and sincere people still disagree on some passages. Good reading holds firm convictions with humility.
46205: Interpretation is unavoidable: every reader brings questions, language and culture to the text. The goal is to let the text correct us rather than echo us.
46206: A text cannot mean today what it could never have meant to its author and first audience, though its meaning can grow deeper as God's story unfolds.
46207: Genre matters: a psalm, a law, a proverb, a parable and a vision each work differently and must be read by their own rules.
46208: Context is king: read whole paragraphs, chapters and books, not isolated verses.
46209: The Bible grew up inside Israel's covenant life. Jewish ways of reading (midrash, wordplay, linking texts, story) shaped Jesus and the apostles.
46210: Christians read the whole Bible as one story that finds its goal in Christ, but this must not erase the Old Testament's own voice.
46211: The Spirit and the community of believers, past and present, help us read; humility, patience and charity help us disagree well.
46218: The world of interpretation: what we read, and how
46219: This map shows the main things a reader must pay attention to (the text, its author, its first audience, its genre and contexts, the whole canon, Christ, the Spirit and the community) and the main methods Christians and Jews have used to read it. Colours show the era that put the most weight on each idea, though most ideas are older than the era that named them. Arrows show how they relate.
46222: The words of Scripture as we have them, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, and in translation. Every method begins here. When Ezra read the Law, the Levites helped the people understand it, so reading and explaining belonged together from the start.
46225: Christians believe each book has a human author writing in a real time and place, and that God speaks through that human voice. The Reformers stressed that the meaning the human author intended is the anchor of interpretation. Many add that God may intend more than the human author fully saw.
46228: The people who first heard the text: exiles in Babylon, a church in Corinth, Israel at Sinai. The Bible was written for us but not first to us. Asking what they would have heard keeps us from reading our own world into theirs.
46230: Genre is the kind of writing: story, law, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, apocalyptic vision, gospel, parable or letter. Each has its own rules, like the difference between a news report and a love song. Modern form criticism made genre a central question, though wise readers always noticed it.
46232: The words around a passage: the sentence, paragraph, chapter, book and its flow of thought. Literary and narrative approaches teach us to notice structure, repetition, characters and plot. Most famous misreadings come from ignoring the verses next door.
46234: The world behind the text: empires, customs, family life, temple, honour and shame, patronage, farming, money. This background explains what words and actions meant then. Archaeology and ancient writings help us see it.
46236: The canon is the collection of books the church receives as Scripture. Reading a passage within the whole Bible lets Scripture interpret Scripture. Brevard Childs' canonical approach stressed the final shape of the books as the church received them.
46238: The Bible's big story is about a faithful God who binds himself to a people by covenant: with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, David, and the promised new covenant. Each passage sits somewhere in this unfolding relationship. Knowing where helps us know how it applies.
46241: Jesus taught that Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms speak of him. Christians therefore read the whole story as reaching its goal in his life, death, resurrection and reign. How directly each text points to him is debated.
46242: Christians believe the Spirit who inspired Scripture also opens readers' minds to understand and obey it. This is called illumination. It does not replace study; it gives understanding, conviction and love.
46244: We read with the church past and present: creeds, teachers, other cultures and the local congregation. The Jerusalem Council read Scripture together to settle a hard question. Tradition can guide, and it can also need correcting by Scripture.
46246: Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus and Tertullian summarised the apostles' teaching (one God, Creator; Jesus Christ, born, crucified, risen; the Holy Spirit) as a 'rule' or measuring line for reading Scripture. Interpretations that broke this rule were judged wrong. The creeds grew from it.
46248: We bring our own language, culture, questions and blind spots. Modern philosophers such as Hans-Georg Gadamer showed that no reader is neutral. Being honest about our starting point is the first step to hearing the text afresh.
46250: The goal of reading is not only knowledge but faith, love and obedience. Application asks how the passage's principle now shapes belief, worship, character and life together. It should flow from the meaning, not replace it.
46252: Midrash is Jewish searching of Scripture, linking texts and filling gaps to draw out teaching. Pesher, found in the Dead Sea Scrolls, reads prophecy as fulfilled in the reader's own community. Both shaped how the New Testament quotes the Old.
46254: This approach reads the Bible as its first Jewish hearers did: as the story of a God in loyal, covenant relationship with a people, with Torah as a gift within that relationship, and with Jesus as a Jewish teacher using Jewish methods and idioms. Writers such as Marvin Wilson, Lois Tverberg and Kenneth Bailey popularise it.
46256: Allegory finds a second, spiritual meaning in the details of a text, beyond the literal story. Philo of Alexandria and later Origen used it widely. Paul uses an allegory once, of Hagar and Sarah. Its risk is that the reader's ideas replace the author's.
46258: Typology sees real people, events and institutions in Israel's history as patterns (types) that God repeats and fulfils more fully later, especially in Christ. Adam, the Passover, the manna and the bronze serpent are examples used in the New Testament. Unlike allegory, it keeps the history.
46261: Medieval Christians read texts in four senses: literal (what happened), allegorical (what to believe), moral (what to do) and anagogical (what to hope for). Thomas Aquinas insisted all spiritual senses rest on the literal. Jewish readers later spoke of four levels too (PaRDeS).
46263: This method seeks the plain sense the human author intended, using grammar, word meanings, genre and historical setting. It has roots in the school of Antioch and the Reformers and is the standard evangelical method. Its weakness can be stopping at 'then' without reaching Christ or 'now'.
46265: This approach, developed in Reformed biblical theology (Geerhardus Vos and others), reads each passage by its place in the unfolding history of salvation: creation, fall, Israel, Christ, church, new creation. It asks what God was doing at that stage of the story.
46267: Christ-centred readings look for how every passage relates to Christ. Some find him predicted or present in many texts; 'Christotelic' readers (like Peter Enns) prefer to say the Old Testament's story has its goal (telos) in Christ, seen most clearly after the resurrection. The debate is about how, not whether, Christ matters.
46269: A family of methods (source, form and redaction criticism and others) that study how texts were written, edited and passed on, treating the Bible like other ancient writings. It has uncovered much about language and history. Critics fear it can silence the Bible as Scripture when used with naturalistic assumptions.
46271: Associated with Brevard Childs, this approach reads books in their final form as Scripture for the believing community, rather than only reconstructing earlier sources. It values the shape and order of the canon as meaningful.
46273: Narrative criticism studies biblical stories as stories: plot, character, point of view, timing, repetition and silence. Robert Alter and others showed how artful Hebrew narrative is. It helps readers notice what the storyteller is doing without moralising every detail.
46275: Reader-response approaches stress the reader's role in making meaning. Moderate forms note how texts invite responses; strong forms (Stanley Fish) say meaning is produced by communities of readers. It exposes hidden assumptions but can lose the text's ability to challenge us.
46277: Theological interpretation of Scripture (TIS) reads the Bible as God's word to the church, using Christian doctrine, creeds and the history of interpretation alongside history and grammar. Kevin Vanhoozer, Daniel Treier and others lead this movement.

46309: A nine-step method for reading any passage
46310: Walk through these steps in order the first few times. With practice they become a habit. The first five steps listen to what the text meant then; the last four ask what it means within the whole Bible and for us now. Prayer belongs at every step.
46312: Read the passage slowly, several times, in more than one translation if you can. Write down what it actually says before deciding what it means.
46313: Who is speaking, to whom, and about what?
46314: Which words or ideas are repeated?
46315: What surprises me or confuses me here?
46316: What does the text not say that I assumed it said?
46318: Decide what kind of writing this is: story, law, song, wisdom saying, prophecy, vision, gospel, parable or letter. Genre sets the rules, as a recipe and a poem do in daily life.
46319: Is this telling a story, giving commands, praying, teaching wisdom, warning, or describing a vision?
46320: Is the language plain or figurative (pictures, poetry, exaggeration)?
46321: How do other passages of this kind work?
46323: Read the whole paragraph, the chapter, and ideally the whole book. Trace how the passage fits the author's flow of thought.
46324: What comes just before and just after?
46325: What question or problem is the author addressing?
46326: Does a word like 'therefore' or 'but' link this to something earlier?
46327: Explore the historical, cultural and Jewish context
46328: Ask what the first hearers knew that we do not: their history, customs, religious practices, and the Jewish ways of thinking and speaking that shaped both Testaments.
46329: What was happening in Israel or the church at this time?
46330: What customs (honour and shame, family, patronage, temple, feasts) lie behind this?
46331: How would a first-century Jew or an Israelite under the covenant hear these words?
46332: Is there an idiom or figure of speech here?
46333: State what it meant to them
46334: In one or two sentences, say what the author was communicating to the first audience. This is the anchor: a text cannot mean today what it could never have meant then.
46335: What did the author want these hearers to believe, feel or do?
46336: Can I state it without mentioning myself?
46337: Would a careful first-century (or ancient Israelite) listener agree with my summary?
46338: Place it in the covenant story
46339: Locate the passage in the Bible's unfolding story: creation, fall, the covenants with Abraham, Israel and David, exile and return, Christ, the church and new creation. Different covenant settings change how a command applies.
46340: Where in God's story does this passage stand?
46341: Which covenant is in view, and how does the new covenant relate to it?
46342: How do later passages pick up this theme?
46343: See how it relates to Christ
46344: Ask how this passage relates to Jesus: as promise, pattern (type), contrast, preparation or direct teaching. Do this honestly, without forcing him into every detail.
46345: Does the New Testament quote or echo this passage?
46346: Does it show a need, pattern or promise that Jesus meets?
46347: How does Jesus' life, death and resurrection change how I read it?
46349: Identify the timeless truth about God, people and life with God that the passage teaches. A good principle is clearly in the text, true across the Bible, and relevant to both the first audience and us.
46350: What does this show about God's character and ways?
46351: Is the principle taught elsewhere in Scripture?
46352: Is any part of the passage tied only to its original situation?
46354: Ask how the principle shapes faith, worship, character and relationships now. Test your application with others in the church and with the wider Christian tradition, and then act on it.
46355: What would obedience look like this week, for me and for us together?
46356: Does my application respect the meaning I found, or replace it?
46357: What do other believers, past and present, from other cultures, see here?
46358: How does this lead me to love God and neighbour?
46359: What kind of passage am I reading, and how should I read it?
46360: Answer a few questions about the passage in front of you. The tree will name its likely genre and give you reading tips. Some passages mix genres (Jeremiah has stories, poems and letters), so try the tree on a paragraph at a time.
46362: What is the passage mainly doing?
46363: Telling a story with people, places and events
46366: Delivering a message from God or describing visions
46367: Teaching wisdom about how life works
46369: Israel's history or the early church (Genesis to Esther, Acts)
46370: The life, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus
46371: A short story Jesus tells to make a point
46372: Who is the poem addressed to?
46373: To God, or to worshippers about God (praise, lament, thanks)
46374: To a beloved, or reflecting on life and suffering
46375: To Israel or the nations, from a prophet
46377: In the Law given to Israel (Exodus to Deuteronomy)
46378: In a letter to a church or a church leader
46379: In a short saying in Proverbs
46380: In Jesus' teaching in a Gospel
46381: What does the message look like?
46382: A prophet calls Israel back to the covenant, with warnings and hopes
46383: Strange symbols: beasts, numbers, heavenly scenes, cosmic battle
46386: Long speeches, debates or reflections (Job, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs)
46388: Read the whole story, not just a scene. Narratives usually show rather than tell: the narrator often reports what people did without approving it. Ask what the story reveals about God and his covenant purposes before asking which character to copy. Watch for repeated words and the narrator's rare comments (such as 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes').
46390: Torah means 'instruction' and was given to a people God had already rescued, as part of a covenant relationship. Read it as a gift that shaped a holy nation. Ask what each law reveals about God's character and justice. Christians differ on how the laws apply now (moral, civil, ceremonial categories; or the whole Law fulfilled in Christ), but all agree Jesus summed it up in love of God and neighbour.
46392: Psalms are poetry, written to be sung and prayed. Expect parallel lines that repeat or contrast an idea, and strong images. Laments give honest words to pain and anger; they model prayer, not doctrine about God's failure. Ask what kind of psalm it is (praise, lament, thanksgiving, royal, wisdom) and pray it yourself.
46394: Read the whole argument. In Job, the friends say many true-sounding things that God finally rejects, so a single verse may be a wrong view. Ecclesiastes tests life 'under the sun' and lands on fearing God. The Song celebrates love; it has also been read as a picture of God and his people. Ask what the book as a whole concludes.
46395: Proverbs are short sayings about how life generally works, not promises or guarantees. Some deliberately pull against each other so that the reader learns to judge the situation. Read a proverb alongside others on the same topic, and ask what kind of person it trains you to be.
46396: Most prophecy is covenant preaching: calling Israel back to faithfulness, warning of judgement, and promising restoration. Only a small part predicts far-future events. Many warnings are conditional. Ask what was happening then, which covenant blessings or curses are in view, and how the New Testament reads the promise.
46397: Apocalyptic writing ('revealing') uses vivid symbols, numbers and heavenly scenes to show who really rules history, especially to suffering believers. Do not read it like a newspaper; ask what each symbol meant in the Old Testament and in its first setting. Christians read Revelation in several ways (preterist, historicist, futurist, idealist), but all agree its message is that the Lamb wins.
46398: The Gospels are ancient biographies with a purpose: to show who Jesus is so that readers trust him. Read each Gospel on its own terms (what Mark stresses is not what John stresses), notice the Old Testament echoes, and read Jesus' teaching in its Jewish setting. Compare parallel accounts to see each writer's emphasis.
46400: Parables are short stories that surprise and challenge. Find the main point or points, usually tied to the audience Jesus was answering; do not turn every detail into a symbol. Ask who the first hearers would identify with, and where the twist comes.
46402: Letters answer real situations, so reconstruct the questions behind them (Paul often says 'now concerning'). Follow the argument from start to finish, and notice how theology leads into practice. Ask which instructions express timeless principles and which apply them to local customs, and do this consistently.
46403: How God's people have read Scripture: a history of interpretation
46404: Ezra reads the Law and the Levites explain it
46405: After the return from exile, Ezra reads the Torah aloud to the people in Jerusalem while Levites 'give the sense' so that the people understand (Neh 8:8). Many see here the roots of public reading with explanation, and of translation into Aramaic. Date approximate (around 445 BC, in Nehemiah's time).
46407: The Dead Sea Scrolls community writes 'pesher' commentaries (such as the Habakkuk Pesher) that read the prophets as speaking directly about their own community and the last days. The copies date from roughly the first century BC.
46409: Rabbinic tradition credits Hillel the Elder (active around the turn of the eras) with seven rules (middot) for interpreting Torah, including 'light and heavy' (an argument from lesser to greater) and linking passages by shared words. The lists appear in later sources (Tosefta Sanhedrin 7.11, the Sifra introduction, Avot de Rabbi Natan 37); how far they go back to Hillel himself is debated.
46411: Philo (about 20 BC to AD 50), a Jewish philosopher in Alexandria, reads the books of Moses allegorically, finding in them truths about the soul and virtue that fit Greek philosophy, while still keeping the commandments. His method strongly influenced later Christian readers in Alexandria.
46413: After his resurrection, Jesus explains to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and then to the eleven, how Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms speak of him, and opens their minds to understand (Luke 24:27, 44-45). Jesus also argues with Jewish methods such as lesser-to-greater reasoning. The year is approximate (AD 30 or 33).
46415: Paul reads Israel's wilderness story as 'examples' (typoi) for the church (1 Cor 10:6, 11), Adam as a 'type' of Christ (Rom 5:14), and Hagar and Sarah 'allegorically' (Gal 4:24). His use of the Old Testament shows Jewish methods transformed by faith in the risen Messiah. Galatians is dated between about AD 48 and 55.
46417: Origen of Alexandria, in *On First Principles* Book 4 (around 220 to 230), teaches that Scripture has a body, soul and spirit: literal, moral and spiritual senses. He was also a careful textual scholar (the Hexapla). His allegorical readings were influential and controversial.
46419: Teachers linked with Antioch, especially Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia (about 350 to 428) and John Chrysostom (about 347 to 407), stress the historical sense and the author's flow of thought, while allowing 'theoria', a spiritual insight grounded in history. Older textbooks set Antioch against Alexandria sharply; recent scholars (such as Frances Young) show both schools shared more than once thought.
46421: Augustine begins *On Christian Doctrine* in 397 and finishes it in 426 or 427. He teaches readers to know the languages, history and figures of speech, to read unclear passages by clearer ones and the rule of faith, and that any reading which does not build love of God and neighbour has not yet understood Scripture.
46423: Rashi of Troyes (1040 to 1105) writes commentaries on the Torah and Talmud that remain central in Jewish study. He weighs 'peshat' (the plain, contextual sense) alongside rabbinic midrash. His work influenced Christian scholars too, including Nicholas of Lyra, whom Luther read.
46425: Medieval Christian teachers summarise the four senses in a famous Latin rhyme (attributed to Augustine of Dacia, about 1260): the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral sense what to do, the anagogical sense what to hope for. The four senses go back to John Cassian (*Conferences* 14.8, about 420s).
46426: Aquinas grounds the senses in the literal
46427: Thomas Aquinas, in the *Summa Theologiae* (part I, question 1, article 10), teaches that God, the author of Scripture, can signify through events as well as words, but that all spiritual senses rest on the literal sense, and only the literal sense can be used to prove doctrine.
46429: Erasmus publishes the first printed Greek New Testament to be put on sale, with a fresh Latin translation and notes. The Renaissance call 'back to the sources' sends interpreters to the original languages, preparing the way for the Reformation.
46430: Luther and Calvin: the plain sense
46431: Martin Luther publishes his German New Testament (1522) and insists on the plain, grammatical sense, 'Scripture interprets itself', and Christ as the centre of Scripture. John Calvin (*Institutes*, 1536; Romans commentary, 1540) prizes brief, clear exposition of the author's meaning and the inner witness of the Spirit.
